projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Edward Somerville was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What business were you in up in Wilmington?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I got to think a minute. What the hell was I doing up there? I worked for Ford Motor Company.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, you did?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Out of Chester?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. Then we moved -- then Edsel came in, and I -- I thought, Boy, I've got it made. I was one of the first employees of Edsel. And I worked out of the -- the City Line Avenue. What did we call this place? We still had -- we still had a place -- that's Chester -- the assembly plant was still working in Chester at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: For Edsel or for --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. They never built Edsels there. The Edsels were all -- all built in New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I went across -- I came across -- I did this movie that we did here in Delaware called Dead Poets back in the late '80s --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Dead Poets Society.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Dead Poets Society. And one of my jobs was to deal -- was that era of cars. And -- and looking around, there's a guy out -- outside of Lancaster, probably closer to Wilmington than towards Lancaster, who's got this farm. He must have two, three hundred Edsels that are sitting there on all kinds of different repairs. He's got the good ones in -- stacked, you know, on -- on different levels. I mean, some of them look brand new. They're still -- still in good condition, and he's got barnyards full of them. I mean hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of Edsels.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Do you remember the gearshift on the Edsel?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I must have went -- I must have traveled 10,000 miles the first year, teaching people about those things, you know. They were so simple. It was just a matter of planetary gears, you know. But, you know, they'd have a problem and -- we can't get it. So, okay, I'll jump in my car and I'll come out, and I held schools on them. But the Edsel was really a disaster, I'll tell you. The best thing we ever had with Edsel is -- I went to school for, like, months, and I -- I grew up in a Ford dealership family. You know, I've been around cars all my life. And the other grandfather was a farmer, and I spent a lot of time on farms, but we used -- we used to go to Henry Ford --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Hold this for a second. (Microphone adjustment.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: We used to go to Henry Ford's Museum every summertime, you know, and never -- I never got enough of that. And then when the Edsel division came along, we had schools. (Microphone adjustment.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I'll stop talking.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Your shirt pulls and -- (Microphone adjustment.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Thanks. Okay. So --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I'll stop talking any time you say.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Go ahead. So you were -- you were in -- in Ohio on a farm?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. Well, one side of -- one grandfather was a farmer, and the other was a Ford dealer, so I grew up in the best of two worlds.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You probably drove the Chrysler when you were probably 10 to 12 years old, too, probably when you were able to do that.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: That's right. And believe it or not, I'm the oldest of 41 grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Really. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: We had 29, so I thought I was -- I thought I was big. I was the oldest of -- I'm the oldest of 29 of us that are all damn near still here.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well -- and we had -- it hasn't been too long ago that our reunion stopped, but my grandmother, when she was too -- 103, Dolly?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: When she was 103, she was involved in an automobile accident. She wasn't driving; she was riding. And that hastened her death. And up until that time since World War II, the nearest Saturday to her birthday, we had a family reunion. We'd have 300 people there. You know --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: -- when, you know, you're oldest of 41 grandchildren, you know --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, I --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: It's a hell of a lot of people.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah, because just us alone, just in my brothers and sisters, seven of us, we had 28 or 29, too, so that's just from the one. So we've got -- out of the 29 of us -- out of the 29 of us, there was only seven that had 29 more for us, so we have a whole bunch of them, too, and I have -- I have -- I have five grandkids myself. I ended up with -- I have six children. The oldest is 37, 38; the youngest is 18.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I had a son. I showed you the picture of my grandson in West Point. His father went to college through General Motors Institute; in other words, he went -- got a job on the assembly line, and they sent him to college. And -- and he did real well, but I haven't figured him out yet. After he retired from General Motors and all that, he became a Baptist minister. And here's a guy that used to race cars with me and all that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: And I -- and I -- I just -- I just can't believe that, you know, now he's a Baptist minister. 3RD SPEAKER: Okay. T.J. --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yes. 3RD SPEAKER: -- we're ready.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Here's what we're going to do: When I ask you a question, repeat the question or repeat -- like if I say, Were you drafted, or whatever, and you say, No, I wasn't drafted, I joined, or whatever.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Where did you go to college? I went to college by where I went to school or I grew up. Where did you grow up? I grew up -- so you have to answer -- because nobody's going to hear me.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It's all going to -- they're all -- they're only going to hear on the final documentary is you.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: They're not going to hear me asking the questions. So what you need to do is put in -- like when I was -- when -- when we first shipped out overseas or when I did this, when I did that, and you sort of answer -- I mean, you sort of say -- stating the question and answering it also. Okay?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, we're going to first start off -- you're going to tell me your full name, spell your last name, where you were born and raised.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You ready?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I'm -- I'm John E. Somerville. I was born in a small town in Ohio -- Frazeysburg, Ohio, which is in the southeastern part of the state. My mother's people were farmers, and my father's people were automobile dealers, and I grew up in the best of those two worlds.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many brothers and sisters did you have?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I have one brother and one sister.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. I'm going to go back to -- what I'll -- I'm going to ask you now is Pearl Harbor day. Do you remember it? Where were you? What were your thoughts about it?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes, I remember it. I was quite young, but in our town (inaudible) fractured drapes in the post office, in the bank, in all kinds of buildings like that, and yes, I was very aware of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How old were you then? That would have been '41.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: '41? I was born in '24, so if you can do the arithmetic --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Seventeen.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Seventeen.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Seventeen.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And you were in high school?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I was in high school.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And do you remember what you were doing that day when you heard about it?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Not -- not really. It was so unbelievable that -- that some of it is very vague, but I was -- wanted to fly airplanes when I was growing up, and I'd work up $10, and I'd get on my bicycle and go out to the local airport and get a ride. And I did it so much, they got very nice. They'd let me -- the airplanes in those days had controls. They were open -- open airplanes, but they had controls on the front and the rear. And it got to the point they would let me fly a lot. And the more I did that, the more I wanted to be a pilot in the Air Force. So they came out with a program that if you could pass a two-year college equivalent examination, then you could be accepted. So I went to -- I was sent to Wheeling, West Virginia, which was not that far from Southern Ohio, and took the examination. And I passed it and I was sent to another -- another place in Columbus, Ohio, where I did another physical. And that's where I was -- finally passed everything I needed to do and was sent to flying school. Now, my life -- my flying training was all in the -- what they call the "Southeast Training Command." First, we went to what they called a "Classification Center," and they asked some of the weirdest questions I've ever been asked in my life, that I won't even repeat here. But this is where they determined where you'd be a pilot, a bombardier or a navigator. They even went down to the point to -- they -- there they determined whether you would be a fighter pilot or a bomber pilot or a transport pilot or what -- whatever. Then after -- and I got there at a very bad time. We had a great outbreak of spinal meningitis. They hung sheets between all the -- the beds in the rooms that we lived in, and all daylight hours we marched. They wanted to get us out in the open, you know, and we marched and we marched. And I'm telling you, when we went to flying school, there's one damn thing we could do: We could march. But it was good training. I -- I think it taught you the discipline that became necessary. In -- in a fighter organization, discipline is so, so important. You're out there, usually 12 of you, sometimes 16 of you, and one-word command, you know, two-word command, everybody's got to do it and they got to do it then. So it took a lot of training until you really got to the point to be able to be a fighter pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Could you -- could you actually fly before you went in?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You played around with the planes --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- but you never really --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Just went out -- and we had an airfield about 10 miles away, and I'd ride my bicycle there when I got -- the flights were always $10. Well, I'd get $10, and they would take you up for ten minutes. And after a while -- and they had controls of -- you sat in the rear cockpit, and the pilot sat in the front, and they had controls in both. And after you went a lot of times, they'd let you take the controls, and they'd tell you to do this and do that. So when I first got -- gotten my first military airplane, it wasn't all new. I had been through that, not much, but I'd been through a portion of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Uh-huh. So where was your flight training? Where -- where did you take your flight training?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, the last school I was in was Dothan, Alabama; that was the last place. And that's when we got into a P-40 for a few hours. The first one was in Tennessee, and I just can't place the -- this was a very, very small field. We flew PT-17s, which were -- was a twin-engine airplane, no radios. The pilot and the -- the training pilot and the -- and the student, they talked -- they talked through gosports, if you could imagine that. It was rubber tubing, except it got to your ears and was like a stethoscope.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Really. Well, it was -- really. And, hell, half the time you couldn't understand what they were trying to tell you to do, but -- and we got through that phase of it, and we went to basic flying school. There, we had flaps. We had landing flaps, and it was a low, veneer airplane. It was -- it was fixed gear. You couldn't raise or lower the gear.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: We went through that phase of training, which each phase was like 40 hours, as I recall. Then we went to advanced, where we flew AT-6s, and they had landing gear that raised and lowered. They had flaps that raised and lowered hydraulically. We had a propeller that was constant speed; in other words, whenever you wanted, you set your propeller speed, and regardless of how you changed throughout, the speed would always be the same. And it had some guns on the wings, and we got our first gunnery training in that. And while we were there, while we were still cadets, we had some P-40s, which were hopelessly outmoded at that time, and so we used those to fly gunnery. And so when we got into combat, we had a little bit of all experiences.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Where did -- now, when did you squad up -- where did you get into a squad, and where did you guys leave from, and where did you end up?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, I went over as a replacement. You know, this is embarrassing. This is a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I -- believe me --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: We went to -- we went overseas on His Majesty's ship, Tamburello. It was a small, British ship. We went in a convoy. (Clears throat.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you want some water?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Huh? 3RD SPEAKER: There's a fresh bottle here.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you want some water? There's a fresh, brand- new bottle of water if you would like some?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: On the S.S. Tamburello -- the British are terrible. I tell you, the more I got to know the British, the more I hated those bastards.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Get that. Did you get that? (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: But on this ship -- so that's overboard. And we were in a convoy. You couldn't see the edge of the convoy, but every morning, they'd throw these big nets over. Whatever they caught, that's what we ate. We ate fish all the time, and it took us 13 days to go across. And when we got across, we went to a replacement depot in England, and we didn't know they were flying there. We finally got an assignment after the invasion. They flew us over in B-17s to our new assignment.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, what was this? Was -- it wasn't D-Day -- was it D-Day, the invasion? When you said --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. It was after D-Day, a couple of months after D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I can't -- I don't remember. I could look it up --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. That's fine. So you were -- you were -- actually were assigned after D-Day -- after D-Day?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. We were -- we were fighter pilots, and we were trained on P-47s. We didn't all go to P-47s. I was fortunate enough to learn new -- just have P-47s, but some of them had 51s and we -- we were in the 19th -- the 9th Air Force, 19th Tact. Tact. was just a smaller organization. And in the 19th Tact., I think, they were probably four or five different fighter groups. A fighter group was normally three squadrons. My squadron -- well, that's a good question. That's a very good question. But, anyway, we started combat after the invasion. We flew --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You were flying out of England?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. We were flying out of France.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: We lived in tents. Our runways were pierce planking. You might be familiar with pierce planking or not, but they just picked a level place and leveled and, you know, put it together with pins, and that was our landing strips. And we lived -- our tents were very, very close to the -- to the landing strips. Our missions -- you had to become pretty good navigators, because most of our missions, we didn't know what our missions were until we took off. We took off and we got some altitude, and we called -- we had different names of this main -- main area where they -- they knew where they needed help, and they would send us there. And we had to be very good at navigation, because they would just give you a location and they'd expect you to get there. And -- and we had controllers on the ground all over, that -- that if we got in trouble, couldn't find our way home or, you know, our instruments went out or something, they could call us and, you know, bring us back home. If you're low on fuel, they could do that to get you home real quick. The 9th Air Force was very well organized, I guess, is what I'm trying to say. And we -- we consistently flew missions. We flew -- some of them were not easy. Being young -- I was 19 in combat. You know, the older people never -- they were smart. They never volunteered for anything. Well, we were very familiar with George S. Patton because we -- all of our flying against his -- was against his opponents, against the 3rd Army. And we got this request one time to fly a relief mission. General Patton had a full colonel that was stationed over there, and he was surrounded -- surrounded by Germans, and they were running out of everything. And so they -- they picked six of us, and they took -- cut the belly tanks apart and they put in the ammunition, food, blankets, you know, every damn thing. And weather was terrible. We had to get -- we never got over like 300 feet because, you know, we had -- we had nothing. We were so low, that they weren't sure that they could factor us in from far away. So we went around hilltops, you know. We'd stare at blizzard clouds, and we found them and we dropped them. And then a great thing happened. Here's General George S. Patton, who is in charge of the whole 3rd Army and did all kind of great things. One day we got this P-38 pistol, brand new, great German pistol, in the holster and all that. And then the -- a letter had come, issued, which made you think, you know, How the hell did a man like George S. Patton have time to do that, you know? Even though it was his son, you know, but -- but it was a great thing in my life. I was very proud of that. Lost a lot of friends. We had -- I had lost my best friend from Philadelphia, but he ended up -- ended up in a prison camp and eventually got back up to Philadelphia. He and another man, a young man from Philadelphia, and I were real buddies at Dover. And I was the only one who survived. I'll take that back. Chip survived, but he was -- he was never the same again after spending all that time in prison camp. I guess they were -- really treated him terribly and all that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: They were in your squadron?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. It's over -- overseas, we went overseas at the same time, and when we were in a replacement depot in Wilmington -- or in England, we went and said, "Could you put us all in the -- in the same outfit?" Well, they -- we weren't in exactly the same out, but we were in the same group. A group is made up of three squadrons, so -- but we saw each other everyday and all.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember your first mission?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah, I sure do. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I was never so goddamn scared in my life. Yes, I really do. It -- you know, you can -- you can see movies about being shot at and all. But, by God, when you get shot, especially for the first time, you'll never forgot it. Believe me, you'll never forget it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What were your -- what were -- in your first mission -- tell me about your first mission. Go through it a little bit with me.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, I don't really remember exactly the first mission. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The first mission when you were scared to death.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: You were scared to death basically all the time, when I get right down to it. Well, you -- you didn't -- you didn't see what you should be seeing, you know. You were concentrating so hard on flying the wings of another person, that you still had to learn to fly formation and look around and, you know, see where the ack-ack is on the ground, because they shot at us constantly. And the Germans were good shooters. So any time you flew, you always flew like this (indicating), you know, so they couldn't -- because if they really got on you, you were dead; you were gone. In all of our missions, we -- we had to put up with ack-ack. It was there all the time. Enemy aircraft, by this time, not too much of it. They just -- their best had been shot down -- their best pilot had been shot down, really, because there's a lot of them that got shot down over in England and in (inaudible). So that wasn't -- our biggest concern was fire from the ground, not from enemy airplanes, and -- and that you had constantly. If you were -- you had constantly -- The Battle of the Bulge, we were the closest airspace to there. We could get there in about three-minutes flying time, four-minutes flying time. And I never saw anything like that in my life. We -- for different reasons, we had like -- there was times when we couldn't contact somebody, and they could talk to us by panels of different colors, whether they could, you know -- like maybe we'd catch a vehicle out where it shouldn't be, you know. And he -- he would jump out real quick and throw out some panels, and we -- you know, we'd let him go. Otherwise, you know, he was dead. And so then in this Battle of the Bulge, that all went to hell in a handbasket, because they were driving our Jeeps; they were driving our ambulances, our weapons carriers. And, finally, you know, we got some ground controllers up close, and I think one of the hardest things I ever had to do when they said, you know, shoot that ambulance. But, you know, you shot the ambulance and it damn near got you when it exploded, you know. The Germans were using American ambulances, you know, to carry weapons, you know, and all. It was a crazy time. And we were very close to losing the war then. We really and truly -- if General Patton hadn't been able to move his troops when he did -- the weather was absolutely terrible. It was absolutely unreal. But if he hadn't made that, we wouldn't -- in my opinion, we would have lost the war, really and truly.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: During the Battle of the Bulge, how long did it go on?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: About three or four days. I don't remember exactly, but I'd say three or four days.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- and the weather, you mean like snow and just bad weather?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, does that -- how did that deter you guys? Did that deter you pretty good?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, if visibility is zero, if you take off, you'll never land again, you know, safely, because you can't see the runway; nor can you do any damage, because you can't see people on the ground.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: So you have to have some visibility. And for several days we didn't have -- we didn't have that visibility, and so the Germans were able to move on the ground, and there's nothing we could do about it, nothing at all we could do about it. But when we found them, we decimated them, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, that was your mission: To pretty much go in and seek and destroy?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Basically --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- bombs and guns and --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: A normal mission, we would go out and if -- sometimes we had specific missions to go to a certain place and shoot up a certain thing; maybe it was because there were tanks there. And sometimes we went out in what they just called an arm recce. I may have said that before. We just went out looking for trouble. Trains, we'd love to find a train. We would -- we would just sometimes -- sometimes there's humor in war. Germans, to keep us from seeing their trains, they had a way to shut off the steam. And there were times that we'd go out and we'd see them shut off the steam. And we would fly around, you know, like we didn't see them, and see if he'd blow himself before he had cut loose the steam. Either way, we're going down to shoot the hell out of them, you know. But many times, he would stay there until his engine blew up, and then he couldn't move at all. But they were devious too. We would start down, shooting these boxcars; and all of a sudden, the front of a boxcar would fall down, right, and here's two 20-millimeters that are "whoosh-whoosh" right at you.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What kind of range did they have, the 20-millimeters?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: A mile, I guess, or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, the ack-ack?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, the ack-ack, they -- like they -- at 40,000 feet they had ack-ack that would come up there, but we didn't lose many to ack-ack.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And what were they? Basically, a bomb that went off, like almost like a --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: A big shell.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then it would explode when it got to altitude?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. But they were not very successful in shooting us down. They just weren't. They just -- we moved so much. And, you know, if you're at 20,000 feet, hell, you can see the shell coming, you know, from some of those, because they'd leave like a calling trail. Airplanes had the advantage over people on the ground, a big advantage. That's why I'm lucky I was -- that I was able to be a fighter pilot rather than a grunt on the ground.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- so most of your battle missions were actually seek and destroy --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- rather than cover?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Rather than run and --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. The 8th Air Force did the cover out of England.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then the 99th, right?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The Tuskegee guys did, too, right? Didn't they do the cover?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. The Tuskegee guys --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Or were they actually --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I thought they did more -- see, we listened to them on the ground all the time, on the radio. They were on the same frequency, and they were 9th Air Force also.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: But we didn't have that much contact with them. We just knew they were there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, apparently, the squadron at McDream (phonetic) just was -- just were talking about -- were basically bombers, I think. They were run and cover for them.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: They -- they had bombers, they had fighters. I wish I could get you to interview a man we had at the last reunion. You remember him, Dotty? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. He was a black man. He had flown -- and this is no crap -- he had flown almost every damn airplane that the Air Force ever had, and he had a tremendous combat record. And you've heard some of the missions -- like some of the missions he flew that were over water for, you know, so long of distances, you know, and hoping you're going to make it to -- you know, that you're navigation's right; that you're not going to run out of fuel out over the ocean and things like that. I just wish you could interview him.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Is he a Tuskegee pilot?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. He was a Tuskegee pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Still alive today?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: From Ohio or something?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. Do you remember where he's from? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: But I think he was from Alabama, I believe. Where was the Tuskegee reunion?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Alabama.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I'm sure that that's where he lives.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- conflict, that's what (unintelligible) was saying, that when they got the 51s -- I guess they started with the 40 -- what did they start with? The P?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The Tuskegee started with the 48s, and then they ended up with the 51s?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I don't really know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Whatever the last ones they had, apparently had a hell of a range on them. I mean, they --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, the last ones they had were the P-47s.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, is that what it was?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Maybe that's what he's talking about. They turned pretty quickly too?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. That's what he's talking about. I guess, what, the 51s couldn't get out of their own way sometimes?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, the 51 was probably better than we were in escort. They rolled faster. They could accelerate faster, but they were much more vulnerable than we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So when you --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: It being a water-cooled engine.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right. So when you went up -- when you go on your mission -- when you get on your mission, out of your group, how many planes would take off?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Usually 12.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Twelve?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Sometimes 16. Sometimes -- there was a time in the Battle of the Bulge when we went out on four.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Four at a time?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, would you trade off? I mean, would you come back, rest, go back out? I mean, how -- how did that work?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, we had 26 airplanes in a squadron, and we sometimes had as much as 50 pilots. Sometimes we had a lot less, so -- but you usually -- you very rarely flew every day, but usually, like, every third day, you at least flew.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, did you guys have missions like the bomber guys did after so many missions?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: (No response.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You know, like, they had like 25 missions, and basically, they would get X number of points. I mean, did you guys have -- did you guys consider yourself, I mean, like that, like they did?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: A hundred missions, we were --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Is that what it was?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: They went through 25. But, you know, their missions were like kamikaze missions, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: The early part of the war, they really were the -- the fighters or the escorts couldn't go all the way with them, things like that. So Luftwaffe would wait until our escorts had to turn back, and then they'd come on.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many missions did you fly?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: How many, Dotty? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I think it was six -- yeah. I think it was 66 missions that I flew.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, what -- is there one mission or one thing that sticks out in your mind other than the Patton story?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: (Pausing.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I mean, when you got --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Just give me a second here. Okay. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, like when 12 of you go up, would all 12 of you come back most of the time?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No, no. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I mean, you'd lose one or two every time?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, almost really.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. You see, because we were working at low altitudes. We were down to a hundred feet, and the Germans were good. They were good. You know, they were shooting at us from tanks, a lot of aircraft guns. Soldiers -- foxhole shooting at us with a rifle even. The guy shooting with the rifle didn't have much success, but the others did. And like I say, they -- we stopped. We used to do marshalling yards, and they had so much ack-ack at the marshalling yards that we stopped that. We went to trains outside of town. You know, between towns.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I mean, would you fly right into Germany?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Oh, yeah, sure did. Well, we -- we'd start out with targets in France, but yes, we got into Germany. We sure did.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: But during the Bulge, was it hilly? Was there valleys or was it --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: It was -- as I recall -- this is a long time ago, but I would say that it was rolling hills, but that's a long time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: But was it easier -- was it -- was it fairly easy for you to maneuver it? I mean, was there a lot of tricky pull-ups or pullouts or anything?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Oh, no, no. Sometimes -- unfortunately, I lost my film, but I had one film that I was very proud of. I'm going up a hill, and you'd swear I'm going to run into the grass, and I'm shooting at the grass, because I'm pulling back so damn hard and I can't let up on the trigger. It was -- see every time we flew a mission -- and this really hurts me. We -- and we always flew out of tents. But in any event, we had a tiling machine. You know, you took a 16-millimeter film pack.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: And you put your name and mission number, and you'd put 20 seconds on it. Then you went out and your crew chief put it in your airplane. And then when you come back -- that was one of the great social events of a fighter pilot, you know. When we'd get film back, we'd show it to everybody: The crew chiefs, the armorers. Your -- your film would come up, and if it was really a good film, you know, you really did a lot of damage and all. And they'd jump up on the table, "That's my man, That's my man," you know. We were a very close organization. I've seen a pilot go out at the end of the runway and wait till dark for his airplane, because we'd -- when we -- our crew chiefs always met us at the end of the runway, because we normally always landed on pierce planking runways and they were narrow. So we had -- on the P-47 we had a very wide landing gear. So our crew chief would wait for us at the end of the runway, and they'd jump up on the wing and hang on a pedotube, and they would keep us, you know, straight; and we would follow their instructions until we got back to our revetment. Crew chiefs were so loyal. It's hard to explain it, because I've seen a crew chief wait till dark at the end of the runway, because they always met us there; and they'd jump up on the wing, you know, and guide us back in. He knew his pilot wasn't coming back, but they're still waiting, you know. You didn't have enough gasoline, you know, and all of that. This was a sad -- sorry. (Crying.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, no. You want some water?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Let's get back to your film. Do we have any?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. But I wonder -- I wonder -- that film's got to be someplace.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you know where it is? I mean, not just yours, but I mean, it's got to be either down in --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I don't think they saved all those. My, God, it would take a big warehouse.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, a lot of that stuff is still around. There's apparently something -- there is apparently something up at -- and I haven't tracked it down ever yet -- up at New Castle County here, right up at the air base. There, apparently, was -- you know, they had a lot of underground stuff up there. There's, apparently, some place up there that has a bunch of film. Of what, I don't know.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well -- well, we went out and we -- we were flying F-86s there. Well, we flew -- I flew P-47s out of there. I flew P-51s out of there, but the F-86, I flew most out of up there. And, yes, we had -- we had a lot of film. I might still have -- do I have another roll of film around, Dotty? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah, it's all on a 16-millimeter. Okay?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No problem with that.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: But it would be interesting to find -- see, what we're trying to do is -- and I know I can tell you when we get off camera, but -- exactly how some of these interviews are going to go, because your interview will be in whole. It won't show up that way when we -- because we only have two hours. It's only a two-hour documentary, so it's -- it'll be -- it'll be very brief. But the whole purpose of this is to -- is to have it in the archives so if somebody wants to see your whole interview -- and that's where we're trying to keep this thing. This thing isn't going to sit on a shelf. This is going to be archived and be part of the history and be part of the history of the state of Delaware and also in -- in schools. And we're trying to get -- between the University of Delaware and one with the college right now to, sort of, archive it. So when we get done, our next six months of finishing up this, that hopefully some people will be able to go on and continue doing these interviews.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So -- because your interview will be transcribed with my questions -- I mean, you know, we'll -- we'll edit it and edit it, but it will be in the Library of Congress and everything. So it's not just -- this isn't just a movie that's going to sit on a shelf someplace after it's already been played. It's going to be part of the history of history, which should have been done ten years ago. But the film -- and what we do is, if I can find some film like that, is when you're talking about that, is you'll be sort of talking under it. It'll show on there, but I think that -- and especially -- and I bet I can find it. I bet if I look for P -- what were you flying in?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: At the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Is -- I know they've probably got it, but down in the archives, it's just unbelievable the stuff that they have.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, I can tell you I was -- just a minute. Well, anyway, the information I brought is my group -- my squadron, you know. Like we were 19th Tact -- 9th Air Force 19 Tact., you know, 362nd Fighter Squadron. Anyway, I have it there someplace, and I'll be -- I'll be glad to leave that with you --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, I've got a copy.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: -- as long as I can get it back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. I've got a --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: If I don't get it back, you'll be a dead man. (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Let's talk about that.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So after Pearl Harbor -- and we'll go back and this will all be cut back in --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. After Pearl Harbor, you were in high school?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: (No response.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You were in high school when Pearl Harbor happened?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes, but I never went back to high school.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, no, no, no. But you were in Pearl Harbor -- Pearl Harbor had happened; then you were still in high school?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And you wanted to go in?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And tell me about -- tell me about what she was just saying about the story.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: (No response.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You were taking tests?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, yes. Well, I used to go out and get money -- I may have said that before.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. While flying, you were --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: So then it came out -- I don't know how it came out -- in the papers. Anyway, I finally got this information that if you passed a two-year college examination, then you could be -- you could be accepted as a pilot for pilot training. I took -- I had to go to Wheeling, Virginia. Is that what I told you, Dotty, to take the exam?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: And I passed an exam, and they said that, you know, I would receive something later. Well, I got a letter. I swear it was that thick (indicating). And -- still in high school. And down on like page 30, there it says, you know, "Johnny Somerville 15171116." I said, All right. Well, up at the front, it said, "The following officer candidates will report in four days in Columbus, Ohio, on a certain, certain date." And I was quite naive. So there was this colonel. So I wrote him a nice letter that, I'm sorry that I could not report because I did not graduate from high school, so-and-so, right. And I immediately got a letter back. It was very long, really. It was really very lengthy. It said, You will report, you know, whatever date it was. That was the entire letter. You will report, right. So I did, you know, and what a -- for a naive high school kid, you know -- the first thing they do is take all your clothes, right, and there must have been 400 people in this big -- what was they called? Anyway this big area, right. They took all your clothes away. You walked around bare-ass naked for the first time in your life. And you -- you know, you said, What the hell did I get into? Why did I do all of this? It was really tough. I -- I had a hard time, but I don't know how it really happened. But in the Cadet Corps with me was a master sergeant. He was like 27 years old, which was the maximum, and he took me under his arm. First thing he did, he said, "Kid," he said, "Give me them new shirts of yours, and you wear my old shirts." Well, his old shirts had three up and three down (indicating), you know. People didn't bother me anymore, you know, because they really thought I was the youngest master sergeant that had ever been in the Army, right. You know, things like that happened all the time. You know, and these are things that every once in a while you come up -- I can't recall the guy's name now, but if I saw him again, I would recognize him, and I'm sure he would recognize me. We really learned to march. We got an outbreak of spinal meningitis. And we had -- you couldn't see out of where you slept. There was sheets on every place. And at daylight we were outside, and we didn't come back in till dark. And what we did all that time was we marched, and we had this guy who had been a drill instructor, and you know, it got to the point to where we loved it, you know, that we do all these exotic marches, you know. Like there might be six -- whatever you call it, right. Well, he'd give the first one, "about face," the second one, "about face," you know. And then a little bit later, he'd bring us all back and we'd be right together. It was really good for us, because it kept us -- our mind occupied. And kept us in good physical shape because, you know, we were out doing that for hours every day.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What -- let's get back to a -- to your -- your firefights -- or your -- your combat experience. Do you -- was there anything that set you apart from the guys that were shot down, that you feel? I mean, were you more aware of what was going on? Did you make yourself more aware? Did you -- do you think you were better trained? Did you think you concentrated more?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You think it was just a matter of the draw?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I think it was -- yeah, I think it was luck. I really do, because I -- we all were very well trained. If -- if we weren't qualified to be a combat fighter pilot, they found another place for you. You might be flying C-47s or, you know, God only knows; but if you couldn't hit the target, you know, all of these things, then you couldn't fly great -- you didn't end up in those jobs, because it was dangerous.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: John?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: You had told me that when you finished your offices -- when you finished your training pilot, they -- instead of they putting you right into combat, like all of the people that were with you, you were -- they -- they sent you to Delaware as an instructor. And you got so many hours in it; you got extra training.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah, that was later, Dotty.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. I'll take that back.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: You said that's why you weren't shot down like all the others.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. Well -- yes. I was sent to Dover, and I sort of forgot this, but I had a commander. His name was Barry, NMI, no middle initial, Chandler. He came from Louisiana, a fairly prominent family, as I had figured out later. He's the best fighter pilot I ever saw all my life. I reported in and my flights equipment didn't get there. None of my luggage got there. So I reported to the flight line, and here's this pretty well bald-headed guy, pretty big man, and -- and in the tent. And we had P-47s sitting out there on the ramp and, God, they looked big and beautiful. And the guy said, "Somerville?" I said, "Here." He says, "What?" I said, "I'm here." He said, "You see what the hell those are?" And I got it and I said, "Here, sir." He said, "Get suited up." I said, "Sir, I can't get suited up." "Why can't you get suited up?" "Because my luggage didn't get here, and my fly suits didn't get here." "Put this one on." And he was a white colonel. And so I put it on, and I started doing this (indicating.) He said, "What the hell are you doing?" I said, "I'm a second lieutenant." He said, "That's my goddamn uniform. I paid to have that goddamn thing sewed on there; leave them there." Well, I flew that and I was around the flight line for about ten days before they finally found all my stuff and it all came in. And everybody was talking about "that's the youngest lieutenant colonel I ever saw in my life." (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You and your uniforms.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. And I was the second lieutenant. But the first time I went out to fly with this man, he said, "Now just imagine we got a rope between these wings." And this rope was like 20-foot long. He said, "I don't want that rope broken." Now, there really wasn't a rope, you understand. And he went up, and when -- I flew with him and I flew with him. And I was wet from sweat, I'll tell you, the whole thing. And he said, "Now, you know, we're going to take off in formation; and we're going to land in formation; and we're going to fly in formation; and we're going to taxi in, in formation; and we're going to park in formation." I said, "Yes, sir." He said, "Just imagine you got this rope, you know." Okay. Well, we did. And we walked in, among all the other new pilots, and he said, "Somerville, you know, if you can get a couple of hundred hours in that cockpit, you might make a fighter pilot." Oh, God, you know. So that man taught me an awful lot. He was tremendous. When I went to -- he went back in combat. At first I didn't believe him. He said that he's -- he liked me because I fixed his damn car. That's why he really liked me. And he -- well, first, we went to Wilmington. He said, "Let's go to Wilmington, you know." We got to the hotel -- it's no longer there -- and we went there and went to answer the phone --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Rodney -- Hotel Rodney?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: That's right. Anyway, we had a couple of escapades in there, you know, with -- some people did him -- didn't give him the right respect. But we got out without a fight. We didn't get aggressive or anything. But then -- let me see, what was the next -- oh, he was saying, you know, about his friend Shorty. Anyway, he was the overall general of the whole East Coast of the Army Air Corps. I can't remember his last name right now. But he said, you know, "He's a friend of mine." Well -- so he says, "This is good." He says, "Shorty's going to come down and visit us." So the base commander, he's a bird colonel, and he's scared to death of the general, you know. So General Landon, and we're all there, you know, we've got to see what's happening, you know. And so Shorty got out of the airplane. He went right back to the general and said, "Shorty, how in the hell are you doing, you know; you're doing a good job down here. That's what I hear, you know." And that poor general base commander -- the only time in my life I ever felt sorry for him, I felt sorry for him right then, because he was, you know, completely ignored, and he was the big man on the field. But there were generals like that. In fact, I tell you what, it was easier to be a grounded general than it was the captain. I mean that sincerely.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. Now, when you finished, did you go back -- when you were instructing, you went back into combat from Dover?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. That's -- that was before I went into combat.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, that you were at Dover?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. I was an instructor before I went.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right. So you got a lot of experience doing that?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. I went over -- I went overseas with more hours than a lot of people came back from overseas with.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you literally left out of Dover --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- to go overseas? That's -- (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: It was -- it was -- it was a great -- great help.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Let's see. What do you want the generations to come to know and remember about World War II?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: That it was unnecessary and lost us many, many good people, and I don't know where -- I don't know. I don't know whether we accomplished anything or not. We lost a lot of people, but I don't think we accomplished that much. I don't know. I -- I have mixed emotions about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Would you do -- would you do it again? Would you --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Absolutely. Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me in your words, like, I would absolutely --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: If there were another war and I could join up, I would. I would feel bad if I wasn't able to. I know at my age I can't be a fighter pilot anymore, but I can be a great instructor. I still have the ability to fly fast airplanes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you still fly?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. But I -- but I really feel that if I had maybe ten hours of T-33 with an instructor pilot, you know, then I'd be off to the races. I could do whatever I did before. But, you know, it's a feel and you have to get the feel for that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I'll never forget when I made my first solo landing -- or when we were landing or learning how to land.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It's just all of a sudden -- you know, you could do -- what my instructor used to say -- nice landing bouts. You take off, but all of a sudden -- then you get to feel the stick, and all of a sudden there was a good one, and every time afterwards, a good one, a good one, a good one, you know. It's just like you said, it's "the feel."

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I saw it in PT-17s. I had a good friend, Whitey, and I'm trying to think of Whitey's last name. But we had the same instructor, and I don't know -- I had, you know, flew a few times in the back of an airplane before I -- before I got in. And he was -- he was the most cocky guy I ever knew in my life. And I -- I really loved the guy. I loved to go into town with him. We'd go in and get a snootful and get back and all, but I soloed a PT-17. We had the same instructor, and I soloed that. And Whitey was there waiting to get in, and he got in and he took off and he come around and he come around and he come around and he came around. (Laughter.) So we're all out there, waiving till death -- death -- death (laughter), and he -- and he -- and he finally got -- he finally landed. He hit hard (laughter). He went -- I know he went as twice as high as this room and come back down again (laughter). But by the time he spun it on the ground, it was so slow that everything was all right (laughter). And he turned out to be a hell of a pilot, you know, after that. You know, after he got initiated that first time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What do you think? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. Tell me about -- tell me about the one that was at -- tell me about your squadron, about being the last -- you know, your reunion group. The P-47 guys.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that just -- that was all P-47s from all different -- Dotty, was one guy from my group, from my squadron?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Most of them are dead now.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I know, Dotty. (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So tell me about that and then tell me about the last meeting, or it's going to be the --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: We think the last meeting is going to be in Seattle. I have it in my case over here.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: You want me to get it?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, no, no. I'll get it. You just need to tell me about it.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Okay. It's going to be held in -- Where is it, Dotty? DOTTY: Washington -- in Seattle, Washington.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Seattle, Washington. And it will be our final -- final thing, where we, at that time, will distribute all the memorabilia we have left and that sort of thing. I'll show you later. I have -- in my case there, I have one of our newsletters, and I think on -- Doesn't this say, Dotty, that this is the last newsletter? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: So I'm going to try to get one in New Jersey if I possibly can. You know, they have a little museum over there, so hopefully, we'll get some memorabilia there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How about up in Dover?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Possibly Dover.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you have mixed emotions about Dover?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I got the shits with those people in Dover. They won't let me on the base and, you know --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Really. (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. I just wanted to show her my quarters back there. There were two of us, two fighter pilots, and we were in this brick building that had two rooms in it, right. And in the window we had -- remember they had the stars with people in service. We had two stars in the window, and we had a base commander, and I think the only reason he came in, to make an inspection. And he saw them and he didn't make us take them down. The other end of the room, we had -- he was really a good pilot, but he couldn't fly sober. If he wasn't drunk, he would taxi out to the end of the runway and turn the mags completely off, you know, so it would backfire and all the commanders rised [sic] up. And when he was able to come back drunk and take off, he could fly and, man, he was good, but he had lost his nerve. He just couldn't fly sober. He'd come in -- he had a '41 Ford -- I'll never forget it -- and he'd come in from town or the officer's club every night, boom, you know, he was there and he ran right into the building. It was a sturdy building, you know, and he never put a hole in a chair or anything. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did you retire out of the Reserves -- out of the National Guard?

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: No. I quit.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did you stay --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, I retired, yes. But I didn't get a pension or anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. Just like my dad didn't.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I -- the paperwork is there.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: He was a major when he retired.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What do you say? Good? (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. Just tell me -- let's go through the -- tell me about the last meeting -- you don't have to tell me where you guys are going to be -- the last meeting for the P-47 guys and -- tell me that again. And it's your last newsletter and -- you tell me that.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I'll give you the last newsletter.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, no, no. That's fine. Just tell me about it.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, our last meeting was in Connecticut, right, Dotty?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Just look at me and tell me that.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Well, I'm --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, that's okay. So now we know it's in Connecticut. But just tell me about the last meeting that's going to come up, which is going to be in Seattle.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So it's a P-47 pilot -- just say, Our P-47 organization is meeting for the last time --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yes. That's going be --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, tell me that. Just say that: Our P-47 --

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: I belong to an association called P-47 Fighter Pilots. We are losing our people at a very rapid rate. I'm one of the youngest, and I'm 81 years old. So we're trying to get together the last meeting. And at the last meeting we will give away all the memorabilia, and we want suggestions like -- well, whether or not we'll give some to the Smithsonian and some to the -- the little place in New Jersey, and -- that would be my recommendations. And the money's -- whatever money's left, we're going to give to charity. Am I right, Dotty?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: No. You're going to give it to all the museums.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Oh, that's right. We're going to give them -- everything left in our treasury, we're going to give to museums that have to do with P-47 aircraft. (Sotto voce conversation.)

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. And then we'll do the side stuff. (Photos taken of Mr. Somerville from either side.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: John Edward Somerville
sp.p: Okay. Thank you.
